questions.question: Explain how drying preserves food, give three examples from southern Africa, and state the conditions for good drying and its limits.
questions.expected_answer: All spoilage organisms need water to feed, grow and multiply; drying reduces the moisture in food below about 15 percent for fruit and meat so that organisms become inactive, though not killed, which is why dried food must be kept dry. Examples: biltong, strips of meat rubbed with salt and vinegar and dried in the cold dry wind of the Karoo; bokkoms, fish split and sun-dried on racks on the West Coast; dried fruit such as apricots, peaches and raisins along the Orange River, as well as dried maize, pumpkin and sweet potato. Good drying is fast enough to beat spoilage but not so hot as to cook the food, using thin slices, moving air, a mesh cover against flies and a dry climate; dried food is light and keeps for months sealed, but its texture and flavour change and it moulds if it becomes damp.

questions.question: Explain the two ways in which salt preserves food, give examples, and state the limits of salting.
questions.expected_answer: Salt rubbed on food or in strong brine draws water out of the food's cells by osmosis, since water moves toward the higher concentration of dissolved salt, and it draws water out of any bacteria or moulds on the food in the same way, so they shrivel; the food dries from within and the water collects as brine. Salt remaining in the food also makes it too salty for most organisms to grow even where moisture remains, so heavily salted food is protected by low water and high salt together. Examples: salted snoek and other fish, corned beef, salt pork and bacon, biltong and salt cod; salt was traded across southern Africa for this purpose. Limits: the food must usually be soaked before eating, too much salt is unhealthy, and some salt-tolerant organisms survive, so salting is often combined with drying or smoking; sugar preserves jam and candied fruit in the same way.

questions.question: Describe the investigation comparing drying, salting and no treatment, including hygiene, method, expected results and how the results are presented.
questions.expected_answer: Six slices of apple or tomato are cut to equal thickness with clean hands and knife, weighed individually and labelled; two are left untreated as the control, two are rubbed generously with coarse salt, and two are dried in the sun under a mesh cover or in a barely warm oven for some hours each day, with all trays otherwise kept in the same room so only the treatment differs. No sample is tasted and all are discarded at the end. Each day at the same time each slice is weighed and its colour, firmness, mould, smell and any liquid are recorded. Expected results in a warm dry room: the control browns, softens and moulds within three to five days; the salted slices lose water into a surrounding brine, stay firm and show little mould; the dried slices lose half or more of their mass in two days, become leathery and show no mould. Mass is plotted against day for the three treatments on one graph, and the conclusion states that both treatments reduce water and prevent the mould seen on the control.
